slides.text: It happened on the 6:40 PM flight from Boston to Heathrow. In my jet-lagged haze at Baggage Claim Seven, I grabbed a battered saddle-brown leather suitcase identical to mine and didn't realize my mistake until I unzipped it at my hotel—revealing oil paints, linen sketchpads, and a scarf smelling of cedarwood and bergamot. On the luggage tag was a phone number and the name 'Soren.'

We met at the airport café on Sunday to swap our bags back, but our flights were boarding at opposite terminals, so we had to leave them with the concierge. Before locking his suitcase, I tucked a tin of my favorite Earl Grey tea inside his coat pocket. When I opened my own bag in Boston that night, I found a small watercolor painting of the Heathrow rain slipped between my sweaters, signed: 'Next Thursday, Carousel Seven?'

For six months of transatlantic consulting, we intentionally took each other’s luggage home every other week, trading books, annotations, and pieces of our lives through customs. Tonight, as the carousel began to spin, my brown suitcase didn't come down the chute. Instead, Soren was sitting right on the moving rubber conveyor belt, holding two boarding passes to Lisbon and grinning. 'I decided to cut out the middleman.'
